title: Question 6
stem: The nuclide $^{3}_{1}\text{H}$ is an isotope of hydrogen that is called tritium.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Determine the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of tritium.

markscheme_points.text: numbers of protons and electrons both = 1

hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the two small numbers in $^{3}_{1}\text{H}$. Think about what the bottom number tells you about charge in the nucleus, and what neutral means for electrons outside.
Hint 2: Think about how the top number counts everything in the nucleus together, so how you can subtract to leave just the neutrons.
parts.proper_answer: number of protons = 1, number of neutrons = 2, number of electrons = 1.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading the nuclide notation**
For any nuclide $^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$, the lower number $Z$ is the proton number. It tells you the number of protons and also the nuclear charge. Here $Z = 1$, so there is $1$ proton.

Step 2: **Finding neutrons and electrons**
The upper number $A$ is the nucleon number, protons + neutrons. So neutrons $N$ is given by $$N = A - Z = 3 - 1 = 2$$ In a neutral atom the positive protons must be balanced by negative electrons, so electrons = protons = $1$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Draw a labelled diagram to represent a simple model of the arrangement of the protons, neutrons and electrons in a tritium atom.

markscheme_points.text: diagram shows 2 neutrons and 1 proton labelled and forming a nucleus
diagram shows 1 electron labelled and separated from the nucleus (not touching the proton and neutrons )

hints: Hint 1: Picture the simple planetary model. Think about which particles sit packed together in the tiny centre and which one sits well away from them.
Hint 2: Count how many of each particle you found in (a)(i) and think about how clear labelling of each circle will show you know what is what.
parts.proper_answer: Central nucleus containing 1 proton and 2 neutrons touching together, with 1 electron shown separate from the nucleus, all particles clearly labelled.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Building the nucleus**
Draw a small central cluster to be the nucleus. Inside it draw three small touching circles: one labelled proton and two labelled neutron. They must be touching or overlapping to show they are bound together in the nucleus.

Step 2: **Adding the electron**
Draw one more small circle well away from the central cluster, labelled electron. It must be clearly separated with empty space to show it is outside the nucleus, for example on a circular orbit around it.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: Tritium is radioactive and undergoes $\beta^{-}$ decay to form an isotope of helium (He). Gamma radiation is not emitted during this decay.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
Complete the equation to represent the radioactive decay of tritium.

$$^{3}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow ^{...}_{...}\text{He} + ^{...}_{...}\beta + ^{0}_{0}\text{X}$$

markscheme_points.text: helium nucleus: top line = 3 and bottom line = 2
beta particle: top line = 0 and bottom line = -1

hints: Hint 1: Focus on the two conservation rules in any nuclear equation. The totals on the top line must match on both sides, and separately the totals on the bottom line must match.

Hint 2: Remember what happens in $\beta^{-}$ decay: a neutron changes, so the total number of nucleons stays the same while the nuclear charge goes up by one. Use this to work out the He numbers first.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Balancing the top line - nucleons**
Nucleon number $A$ is conserved. Left side is $3$. The $\beta$ particle and X have $A = 0$, so all $3$ nucleons must go to helium: $$3 = A_{He} + 0 + 0$$ so $A_{He} = 3$.

Step 2: **Balancing the bottom line - charge**
Proton number $Z$ (charge) is conserved. Left side is $1$. So: $$1 = Z_{He} + Z_{\beta} + 0$$ A $\beta^{-}$ particle is an electron from the nucleus with $Z = -1$. Therefore $1 = Z_{He} - 1$, giving $Z_{He} = 2$. The full He term is $^{3}_{2}\text{He}$ and the beta term is $^{0}_{-1}\beta$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State the name of particle X.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the almost massless neutral particle that must be emitted with a $\beta^{-}$ particle to conserve energy, momentum and lepton number.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remembering the second light particle**
In $\beta^{-}$ decay a neutron becomes a proton plus an electron, but energy and momentum would not balance with only those two. A third particle is also released: the neutral, near-massless antiparticle partner. That is the (electron) antineutrino, written $^{0}_{0}\bar{\nu}_{e}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Determine the quark composition of a tritium nucleus.

markscheme_points.text:
proton: up up down
or
neutron: up down down

hints: Hint 1: Start by recalling the basic building blocks: think about how many up (u) and down (d) quarks make one proton and how many make one neutron.
Hint 2: Now use your nucleus from (a)(i) with its 1 proton and 2 neutrons and add up all the u quarks together and all the d quarks together.
parts.proper_answer: proton = uud, neutron = udd. Tritium nucleus (1p + 2n) = 4 up quarks and 5 down quarks.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recalling single nucleon structure**
You can learn these as a pair. A proton is $$p = uud$$ with charge $+2/3+2/3-1/3 = +1$. A neutron is $$n = udd$$ with charge $+2/3-1/3-1/3 = 0$.

Step 2: **Adding for tritium**
A tritium nucleus has $1$ proton and $2$ neutrons. Total up quarks: $$1 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 = 4$$ Total down quarks: $$1 \times 1 + 2 \times 2 = 5$$ So the composition is $4$ up and $5$ down quarks.
